[PAPER_0018, relevance_score=0.357] Therefore, one of the aims of this study is to test these alternative hypotheses to examine whether positive emotion after reappraisal generation predicts the choice to implement reappraisals at all, and if so if it positively (goal progress) or negatively (goal achievement) predicts those implementation choices.

Another potential indicator of reappraisal effectiveness is reappraisal plausibility, defined as the degree to which a reappraisal reflects what might be actually happening and/or could potentially happen.

[PAPER_0025, relevance_score=0.338] Based on PE's higher predictive power than plausibility in Study 2's positive reappraisal trials and its direct relation to the motive to feel better, we also hypothesized that when having a pro-hedonic motive, PE after generation is a better predictor of implementation choice than is plausibility.

Despite the common assumption that people always want to feel good, empirical evidence suggests that sometimes individuals are willing to sacrifice immediate pleasure in exchange for utility (Tamir, 2016).

[PAPER_0026, relevance_score=0.310] Indeed, in Study 2, participants were more likely to implement self-generated negative reappraisals that were perceived to be more plausible, potentially to gain a deeper understanding of the images. Based on this finding, we hypothesized that when having the motive to understand the stressor (i.e., epistemic motive), plausibility would predict increased likelihood of implementation choice. Furthermore, PE after generation did not predict implementation for negative reappraisals in Study 2, presumably because participants had an epistemic rather than pro-hedonic motive.

[PAPER_0027, relevance_score=0.340] Thus, we hypothesized that when having an epistemic motive, plausibility is a better predictor of implementation choice than PE after generation. Notably, people may not generate many negative reappraisals when not instructed to do so, as they typically do not want to feel worse. As a result, it is likely that positive emotion would still influence implementation to some extent.

We also explored some additional questions.

[PREREG_0001, relevance_score=0.293] Title: Phases of Reappraisal Motive

Description: We are interested in how people decide whether they should implement the reappraisals they generated or not. Specifically, this study asks whether different emotion regulation motives guide people to monitor different things when making reappraisal implementation choices. We hypothesize that people will primarily monitor their positive emotions when having the motive to feel better, but primarily monitor reappraisal plausibility when having the motive to better understand the stressor.

[PREREG_0002, relevance_score=0.401] q2: We hypothesize that in the hedonic condition, positive emotion (PE) positively predicts people's implementation choice and is a better predictor than reappraisal plausibility.

H1: When having the motive to feel better, people are more likely to implement a reappraisal when feeling more positive after generation.

H2: When having the motive to feel better, PE is a better predictor of people's implementation choice than plausibility.

[PREREG_0003, relevance_score=0.357] We also hypothesize that in the understand condition, reappraisal plausibility positively predicts people's implementation choice and is a better predictor than PE.

H3: When having the motive to understand the stressor, people are more likely to implement a reappraisal when it's more plausible.

H4: When having the motive to understand the stressor, plausibility is a better predictor of people's implementation choice than PE.

PE from generation will be entered as a Level 1 predictor to examine whether they predict the choice to implement a reappraisal. Participants will be included at Level 2 and their average PE from generation will be included as a covariate at Level 1.

We will additionally run two binomial regression models for trials in which people are assigned a motive to feel better. In Model 2, plausibility will be entered as a Level 1 predictor. Participants will be included at Level 2 and their average plausibility ratings will be entered as a covariate at Level 1.
